## Exercise 1: Test the gene table with a grouping from the species table

> Pi can run DESeq2 in a minute. Most of the decisions that shape the answer
> come before the test (which samples, which genes, which way round the
> contrast goes) or after it (which cutoff, which plot). Those decisions are
> yours, and this exercise has you look at several versions of each.

Open `notebooks/04-differential.qmd` and run the setup chunk. It reads back the
`community` column you saved on Tuesday and joins it to the metadata. Start Pi
with a fresh conversation.

### Part 1: Predict

1. We will test 13,738 genes. If no gene were truly different between the two
   community types, how many would come out with a raw p-value below 0.05?
2. You will test at week 18 only, which is 157 samples, 37 against 120. Would
   you rather have 157 samples at one visit or 471 samples across three visits?
   Say why before you look at anything.
3. Of the genes that do come out significant, do you expect more to be higher in
   anaerobe-dominant samples or in Lactobacillus-dominant samples?

### Part 2: Ask, look, decide

1. Set up and run the test:

   > Using `d` and `metadata` from the setup chunk, keep only the week 18
   > samples. Keep genes with a count of at least 10 in at least a quarter of
   > those samples. Run DESeq2 on the raw counts with `~ community` and the
   > contrast anaerobe against lactobacillus. Add gene symbols and names from
   > `d$gene_info`. Save the results table to `data/genes_by_community.csv`
   > with the columns `feature` (the Ensembl ID), `baseMean`,
   > `log2FoldChange`, `lfcSE`, `stat`, `pvalue`, `padj`, `symbol` and
   > `gene_name`.

   Tomorrow's notebook reads that file. Before you go on, ask Pi to tell you
   how many samples are in each group (37 and 120), how many genes went into
   the test (13,738), and to print the first five count-table column names
   next to the first five `sample_id` values of the sample table. If those two
   lists are not in the same order, DESeq2 gives you nonsense without a
   warning.

2. A short report:

   > Write a summary of the results: how many genes have `pvalue` below 0.05,
   > how many have `padj` below 0.05, how many of those change more than
   > two-fold, and how many go each way. Then list the top 20 genes by `padj`
   > with symbol, name and fold change.

   Check it against the slides: 1,815 genes at `padj` below 0.05, and 303 of
   them more than two-fold. Read the top 20 names out loud to your group. What
   do they have in common?

3. One result, four plots. From here on, write your own requests. Ask for a
   volcano plot, an MA plot (fold change against mean count), a histogram of
   the raw p-values with a line where they would sit if no gene differed, and
   boxplots of normalised counts for the top six genes by community.

   Check the direction: each boxplot must be higher on the side that the sign
   of its `log2FoldChange` says. Ask Pi to explain the sign convention of your
   contrast first, then compare its explanation with the boxplots. Getting the
   direction backwards is the most common error in this analysis.

4. Cutoffs are choices. Ask for a table of how many genes pass at `padj` of
   0.01, 0.05 and 0.1, crossed with an absolute fold change of 0, 1.5, 2 and 4
   (`log2FoldChange` of 0, 0.58, 1 and 2). Then ask Pi to rerun the test with a
   looser gene filter (at least 10 counts in 10% of samples) and a stricter one
   (in 50%), and to show genes tested, genes significant and how much of the
   top 20 stays the same. Which of these choices changes what you would report?

5. Argue with it. Ask Pi to rerun the test on counts per million instead of raw
   counts. It may do it, or it may round the numbers to make DESeq2 accept
   them. Look at what happens to the results and work out why it is wrong.
   Then ask whether you should have used all 471 samples, and push on the
   answer until it mentions that each person would appear three times.

6. Polish the volcano plot for a talk. Label the ten strongest genes by symbol
   without the labels overlapping. Colour up and down in two colours you
   choose, and put the direction in words under the x axis, "higher in
   Lactobacillus-dominant" on one side and "higher in anaerobe-dominant" on the
   other. Draw dashed lines at your cutoffs and save it as a PNG.

### Discussion

- Did the direction of the effect surprise you?
- What do the top genes have in common? You do not need to know the genes; read
  the names in `gene_name` and describe the pattern in plain words.
- Which cutoff did you settle on, and would a reviewer accept your reason?
- Someone will have used all 471 samples instead of 157. What is wrong with
  that, and how wrong is it?
